title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
why: Maximin share gives each agent a fairness benchmark determined by their own values, independent of how the other agents evaluate the goods. These personal guarantees can conflict when objects are indivisible. The universal constant measures the unavoidable loss from satisfying all agents simultaneously, separating a limitation of fairness itself from a limitation of available algorithms. It is a central quantitative threshold for additive fair division, with significance across instances and arbitrary numbers of participants.
status_note: The January 2026 source explicitly poses this constant. Checked primary statements through 14 September 2026 give the published upper bound 39/40 and a revised-preprint lower-bound claim of 7/9, still far apart at benchmark precision. The 7 September 2026 revision reports a corrected bug; this review verifies its stated scope, not every step of its proof. No matching determination was found in the bounded search.

progress.text: Feige, Sapir and Tauber, Theorem 1, prove the universal upper bound \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\le39/40\) using three agents and nine goods. Their Theorem 3 is tight only within that restricted instance size.

Heidari et al., Theorem 3.1, establish the \(10/13\) additive-goods guarantee. This is the value stated in their own manuscript, rather than the \(7/9\) value grouped with the citation on the problem-list page.
The TCS Open Problems entry asks for the best universal maximin-share approximation and links the additive-goods literature.

Huang and Zhou’s arXiv version 2 states a \(7/9\) guarantee through Theorem 3.1 and the general-instance correspondence in Lemma 2.4; Theorem 10.4 concerns \((7/9-\varepsilon)\)-MMS computation. The revision notice reports a corrected bug. The claimed interval still does not determine the benchmark constant within \(1/100\).

importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: Each agent’s maximin share is the best value they can secure by partitioning the goods and receiving a least-valued bundle.
The target is the largest fraction of those personal shares that can always be met simultaneously for nonnegative additive valuations.
It ranges over all finite numbers of agents and indivisible goods, with equal entitlements and no sharing.
Determining this constant would quantify the inherent loss of fairness caused by indivisibility, independently of computational efficiency.
The card requires a Lean-certified absolute error of at most one hundredth and records the precise versions and limits of the known bounds.

definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.

context_blocks.text: An agent can imagine partitioning the goods into as many bundles as there are participants and then receiving a least-valued bundle. Optimizing that personal partition defines the maximin share. Actual allocation must respect all agents at once, although their best partitions and their rankings of the goods can be different.

The source asks for the best universal approximation and points to results for additive goods. Those linked papers fix the intended valuation class and distinguish it from chores or more general set valuations. The card makes this source-supported interpretation explicit and retains an existence target, without adding a demand for an efficient allocation algorithm.

Feige, Sapir and Tauber give a three-agent, nine-good instance in which every allocation leaves someone with at most \(39/40\) of their maximin share. This bounds the universal constant from above even though its definition includes arbitrarily large instances. Their tight result for that particular pair of agent and item counts is not a tight universal guarantee.

Heidari, Kaviani, Seddighin and Shahrezaei prove a \(10/13\) guarantee. Huang and Zhou’s revised September 2026 manuscript states a \(7/9\) existence guarantee and a fully polynomial approximation scheme for slightly smaller ratios. These are distinct results: the problem-list entry groups their citations under \(7/9\), but the Heidari et al. paper itself states \(10/13\).

The Huang–Zhou revision explicitly reports correction of a bug and substantial rewriting of the proof. Its version and theorem scope are recorded here, without certifying the full proof independently. Computational approximation schemes and stronger results under restrictions on the number of agents remain different from determining the unrestricted existence constant.
